title: MySQL server or driver error text disclosed in a response
description: The response carries a MySQL or MariaDB error raised by the server or by the PHP driver: a refused connection, a dropped connection, or a driver exception class. Unlike a syntax error, these messages name the database host, the driver version and often the credentials path, so a caller learns the deployment shape without sending an injection payload.
remediation: Catch driver exceptions at the application boundary and return a generic error page with a correlation id. Disable display_errors and mysqli exception reporting in production; log the original message server-side only.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the message text; it does not confirm that the database is reachable from the network, and it cannot tell an operator-facing health page from a public one.
scopeT: One response body containing a MySQL/MariaDB connection or driver error string.
fp: A documentation page that quotes these messages verbatim is reported; a health endpoint that returns only a boolean is not.
recordDesc: Database driver errors name the host, the engine version and sometimes the credential source. Echoing them to a client turns a failed query into a map of the deployment, and it gives an injection probe immediate feedback about whether the query even reached the database.
applicability: Responses generated by a PHP, Java or Node service backed by MySQL or MariaDB.
risk: The caller learns the database engine, its version and the internal hostname, which shortens the next step of an attack and confirms which injection syntax the backend will accept.
why: The body contains a MySQL/MariaDB connection or driver error string.
fix: Catch MySQL driver exceptions and return a generic error page.
Set display_errors=Off and log driver messages server-side only.
verifyT: Request an endpoint that forces a database failure and confirm the body carries a correlation id rather than a driver message.

check.valuePattern: (?:Can't connect to (?:local )?MySQL server|mysqli_sql_exception|mysqli::__construct\(\)|MySQL server has gone away|mysql_connect\(\)\s*:)

observation.body: Can't connect to MySQL server on 'db' (111)

title: PostgreSQL connection or authentication error text disclosed in a response
description: The response carries a PostgreSQL connection failure: a failed query handle, a libpq class name, a socket connection error, or the server reporting a failed authentication for a named role. The string identifies the role and the database, which is exactly the information a credential-guessing attempt needs.
remediation: Return a generic error to the caller and log the libpq message server-side. Remove the PostgreSQL host, database and role from any user-visible error page.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the message text; it does not attempt a connection and cannot tell whether the named role still exists.
scopeT: One response body containing a PostgreSQL connection or authentication error string.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the message is reported; a readiness probe returning only a status word is not.
recordDesc: A failed PostgreSQL authentication reports the role it tried, and a failed connection reports the host and port. Serving that text tells the caller both the account namespace and the network position of the database, so the next attempt can target a real account instead of guessing.
applicability: Responses generated by an application whose database driver is libpq or a wrapper around it.
risk: The caller learns a valid database role name and the database host, which turns a blind credential attempt into a targeted one.
why: The body contains a PostgreSQL connection or authentication failure message.
fix: Map libpq failures to a generic error before responding.
Keep the PostgreSQL host and role out of every user-visible string.
verifyT: Force a database authentication failure and confirm the response contains neither the role name nor a libpq message.

check.valuePattern: (?:pg_query\(\): Query failed|PG::ConnectionBad|FATAL:\s+password authentication failed for user|psql: error: connection to server)

observation.body: FATAL:  password authentication failed for user "reporting"

ERROR:  syntax error at or near "SELEC"

title: SQLite driver error text disclosed in a response
description: The response carries a SQLite driver failure: a failed statement handle, an operational or database error class, or a JDBC driver name. These messages name the database file path, which on a single-host deployment is enough to locate the application data directory.
remediation: Catch SQLite exceptions and return a generic error. Never render the database file path in a response.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the message text; it does not read the database file and cannot tell whether the file is still on disk.
scopeT: One response body containing a SQLite driver error string or class name.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the message is reported; a page that mentions SQLite as a product feature is not.
recordDesc: SQLite reports the database path in most of its operational errors. On a single-host deployment that path locates the data directory, and the presence of the driver tells the caller the application is a small-footprint deployment with no separate database to reach.
applicability: Responses generated by a PHP, Python, Java or Node service backed by SQLite.
risk: The caller learns the absolute path of the database file and the deployment shape, which is the reconnaissance step before a path-traversal or backup-file attempt.
why: The body contains a SQLite driver error string.
fix: Catch SQLite exceptions and return a generic error page.
Remove the database path from every error message that can reach a client.
verifyT: Corrupt the database handle in a test environment and confirm the response carries no file path.

title: SQL Server client exception text disclosed in a response
description: The response renders a .NET SqlClient or OLE DB SQL Server exception. The message names the server, the database and sometimes the instance, and the stack frame that follows names the application assembly and its build path.
remediation: Enable custom errors in ASP.NET and return a generic page with a correlation id. Log the SqlException server-side.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the message text; it does not evaluate whether the connection string is reachable from the scanning host.
scopeT: One response body containing a SqlClient or OLE DB SQL Server exception string.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the exception is reported; an API returning a problem+json detail without SQL text is not.
recordDesc: A SqlClient exception carries the server, database and instance name, and the stack frame that follows names the application assembly and its build path. That combination gives an attacker the internal topology and the software identity in one response.
applicability: Responses generated by a .NET or classic ASP application backed by SQL Server.
risk: The caller learns the SQL Server instance, database name and application assembly path, which is the reconnaissance needed to target a second-stage attack or a path traversal.
why: The body contains a SQL Server client exception string.
fix: Return a generic error page from a custom-errors handler.
Log the SqlException server-side and never render its message.
verifyT: Break the connection string in a test environment and confirm the response carries no server, database or assembly name.

check.valuePattern: (?:System\.Data\.SqlClient\.SqlException|Microsoft OLE DB Provider for SQL Server|SqlException: (?:Incorrect syntax|Invalid object name|Incorrect column name))

title: JavaScript ORM query exception disclosed in a response
description: The response renders an error class from a JavaScript data mapper: Sequelize, Prisma, TypeORM or Knex. These classes are developer-visible by design and their messages carry the SQL text, the parameters and the model name, so a public response that includes them leaks both the schema and the data being queried.
remediation: Catch ORM errors in the request pipeline and return a generic error with a correlation id. Map known error codes to user-facing messages instead of rendering the exception.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the class name; it does not prove the query succeeded or that the leaked parameters are still sensitive.
scopeT: One response body containing a JavaScript ORM exception class name.
fp: A changelog or issue page that quotes an error class is reported; a validation error rendered as field-level JSON is not.
recordDesc: JavaScript ORMs name the model, the SQL and the bound parameters in their exception message, and their class names are distinctive enough to identify the stack. Rendering one to a client hands over the schema and the exact query that failed, which is more than a database error: it is a description of the data model.
applicability: Responses generated by a Node.js service using Sequelize, Prisma, TypeORM or Knex.
risk: The caller learns model names, table columns and the bound parameter values of a failed query, which exposes both the schema and the data being handled at failure time.
why: The body contains a JavaScript ORM exception class name.
fix: Catch ORM errors in a single error-handling middleware and render a generic message.
Log the class, message and parameters server-side only.
verifyT: Force a failed query and confirm the response contains no ORM class name, SQL text or parameter value.

title: Framework data-layer query exception disclosed in a response
description: The response renders a data-layer exception from Laravel, Rails, Django or Doctrine. Each of these classes wraps the database message with the query and the bindings, so a public response that contains one discloses the schema, the parameter values and the framework version in a single string.
remediation: Handle data-layer exceptions in the framework error handler and return a generic page. Set debug mode off in production so the exception renderer is never selected.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the exception class name; it does not decide whether the query was user-influenced.
scopeT: One response body containing a Laravel, Rails, Django or Doctrine data-layer exception class name.
fp: A bug-tracker page that quotes the class name is reported; a framework 404 page that names no data-layer class is not.
recordDesc: Laravel, Rails, Django and Doctrine all wrap the database message together with the SQL and its bindings, and they name the framework in the stack. A public response containing one therefore discloses schema, parameter values and the framework version at the same time.
applicability: Responses generated by a Laravel, Rails, Django or Doctrine application.
risk: The caller learns the schema and the bound parameters of a failed query, plus the framework version, which selects the next set of known issues to try.
why: The body contains a framework data-layer exception class name.
fix: Turn debug mode off in production so the detailed renderer is never selected.
Map data-layer exceptions to a generic error page in the framework handler.
verifyT: Force a data-layer failure with debug off and confirm the response contains no exception class and no SQL.

title: Unix password database content served in a response
description: The response body contains the root entry of /etc/passwd in its standard form: the `x` password placeholder, uid and gid zero, the home directory and a login shell. This is the canonical evidence that a path-traversal or a static-file mapping reached outside the web root.
remediation: Fix the traversal or the static mapping that served the file; do not only block the string. Move the web root so it cannot contain parent traversal into /etc, and audit the access log for the request that produced this response.
limitation: One response body. The check proves the file content was returned; it does not identify which parameter or configuration allowed it, and it does not read the file itself.
scopeT: One response body containing the root line of a Unix password database.
fp: A tutorial that includes a sample /etc/passwd line is reported; a page that only mentions the filename is not. The pattern requires the full root entry, not the bare filename.
recordDesc: The root line of the Unix password database is the single most recognisable proof that a request escaped the web root: the `x` placeholder, uid and gid zero, the home directory and the login shell cannot be produced by an application that stayed inside its own content.
applicability: Responses served by a web server, framework or API that maps a client-controlled path to the filesystem.
risk: The caller has read arbitrary files outside the web root, which typically extends to configuration, credentials and private keys; the account list alone supports credential attacks on the host.
why: The body contains the standard root entry of /etc/passwd.
fix: Remove the traversal or static mapping that served the file.
Audit the access log for the request and treat every file read as compromised.
verifyT: Request the traversal path from a test client and confirm the response is a 400 or 404 with no file content.

observation.body: Each line of /etc/passwd has seven colon-separated fields.

title: Windows ini file content served in a response
description: The response body contains the marker line of the Windows win.ini file. win.ini sits in the system directory and has no application purpose, so its presence is evidence of a traversal or a directory-mapping error on a Windows host, the same class as the Unix password database on Linux.
remediation: Fix the traversal or mapping that served the file and review the access log. Restrict the account running the service so it cannot read the system directory.
limitation: One response body. The check proves one file was read; it does not enumerate what else the same parameter can reach.
scopeT: One response body containing the win.ini section marker.
fp: A documentation page quoting win.ini is reported; a page that mentions the filename is not. The pattern requires the marker line itself.
recordDesc: win.ini is the Windows counterpart of the Unix password database for proving a traversal: it sits in the system directory, has no application purpose, and its marker line cannot appear in a response that stayed inside the web root.
applicability: Responses served by a Windows-hosted web server, framework or API that maps a client-controlled path to the filesystem.
risk: The caller has read a file outside the web root on a Windows host, which usually extends to configuration and credential files in the same directory.
why: The body contains the win.ini marker line.
fix: Fix the traversal or the static mapping that served the file.
Run the service under an account that cannot read the system directory.
verifyT: Request the traversal path from a test client and confirm the response is a 400 or 404 with no file content.

observation.body: We still provide support for 16-bit applications on legacy hardware.

title: Location header carries an encoded line break
description: The Location header contains a percent-encoded carriage return or line feed. A server that reflects a parameter into this header without stripping line breaks is one decoding step away from response splitting, and even without splitting the artefact proves the value was not sanitised.
remediation: Reject or strip CR and LF from any value placed in a response header, and validate redirect targets against an allow-list of paths or hosts.
limitation: One Location header value. The check proves an encoded line break reached the header; it does not prove the client or an intermediary decodes it, and no header split is attempted.
scopeT: One Location header whose value contains %0d, %0a or both.
fp: A legitimate Location that carries %0d or %0a as part of a signed payload is reported; a redirect to a clean path is not.
recordDesc: A percent-encoded CR or LF in the Location header means the application copied client input into a response header without filtering line breaks. One decoding step by an intermediary turns that into a second header, which is response splitting.
applicability: Responses that emit a redirect Location derived from a client-controlled value.
risk: An intermediary that decodes the value before forwarding can be made to emit a second header, enabling cache poisoning or script injection under the site origin.
why: The Location header contains a percent-encoded line break.
fix: Strip CR and LF from every value written into a response header.
Validate redirect targets against a fixed allow-list.
verifyT: Send a redirect parameter containing %0d%0a and confirm the Location header contains neither the literal nor the encoded form.

title: Set-Cookie header carries an encoded line break
description: A Set-Cookie value contains a percent-encoded CRLF pair. Cookie values are frequently copied from request data, and an encoded line break in this header is the same unsanitised-input symptom as in Location: one decode step away from injecting an extra header.
remediation: Strip CR and LF from cookie values and encode them with a strict cookie encoder. Never build a Set-Cookie header from raw request data.
limitation: One Set-Cookie header value. The check proves the encoded break reached the header; it does not attempt to make a client decode it.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie value containing the full encoded CRLF pair.
fp: A cookie that stores a signed blob containing %0d%0a by design is reported; a normal session cookie is not.
recordDesc: A percent-encoded CRLF inside Set-Cookie shows that request data reached a response header unfiltered. The Location header gets attention because redirects are obvious; cookies are copied from user input just as often and are less often reviewed.
applicability: Responses that set a cookie whose value is derived from client input.
risk: An intermediary that decodes the value before forwarding can be made to emit a second header under the site origin, enabling cache poisoning or script injection.
why: A Set-Cookie value contains the encoded CRLF pair.
fix: Encode cookie values with a strict encoder and strip CR and LF.
Do not copy raw request data into a Set-Cookie value.
verifyT: Send a cookie value containing %0d%0a and confirm the header carries no encoded line break.

title: Rails detailed exception page disclosed in a response
description: The response carries the marker of a Rails detailed-exception page: a Rails exception class name or the "Extracted source" block. The page prints the request parameters, the session identifiers and the source lines around the failure, so serving it to a client discloses both code and request data.
remediation: Set config.consider_all_requests_local = false in production and render a static error page. Never deploy with the detailed exception renderer enabled.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the page markers; it does not enumerate which parameters the page printed.
scopeT: One response body containing a Rails detailed-exception marker.
fp: A Rails documentation page that quotes the marker is reported; a plain 500 page rendered by the app is not.
recordDesc: The Rails detailed-exception page prints the failing exception, the request parameters, the session identifiers and a window of source code. Serving it discloses the request data of the failing call as well as the application internals, and Rails selects it by default outside production.
applicability: Responses generated by a Rails application running with detailed exceptions enabled.
risk: The caller reads request parameters and session data belonging to the failing request, plus source lines and the exception chain, which is enough to plan a targeted exploit of the endpoint.
why: The body contains a Rails detailed-exception marker.
fix: Set config.consider_all_requests_local = false in production.
Render a static error page and log the exception with its backtrace.
verifyT: Raise an exception in production mode and confirm the response is a static page with no parameters or source lines.

observation.body: Configure a custom error page for production deployments.

title: Symfony exception trace disclosed in a response
description: The response renders a Symfony kernel or debug exception class name. Those pages list the exception chain with file paths and arguments, which discloses the application layout and, for arguments, the values the failing call received.
remediation: Run the application in production mode so the Twig error template is used, and return a generic page with a correlation id.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the exception class; it does not decide whether the arguments printed were sensitive.
scopeT: One response body containing a Symfony kernel or debug exception class name.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the class name is reported; a Symfony-rendered production error page is not, because it names no exception class.
recordDesc: Symfony debug pages print the exception chain with absolute file paths, the request attributes and frequently the arguments of the failing call. A public response that contains one therefore discloses the deployment layout and the data that reached the failure.
applicability: Responses generated by a Symfony application running with the debug kernel.
risk: The caller learns the deployment paths, the framework version and the argument values of the failing call, which supports both targeted injection and path discovery.
why: The body contains a Symfony kernel or debug exception class name.
fix: Run the application with APP_ENV=prod and APP_DEBUG=0.
Return a generic error template with a correlation id.
verifyT: Trigger an exception in prod mode and confirm the response contains no exception class, path or argument value.

observation.body: This application is built with Symfony components.
